clue.text: Wine's gone the wrong way — blow!

explanation.surface: Someone's drink went down the wrong way and they curse it.
explanation.walkthrough: The first half looks like choking on wine; in fact it names the extra glass taken when the decanter is passed back against the usual direction at table.
explanation.definitionFit: In old dining slang this is an extra drink got by passing the bottle backwards; it is also a slap struck with the back of the hand.

clue.text: Movement of a gadabout gad-fly victim

parts.note: read as gad about, the word gad turned round
Io, in Greek myth, was turned into a heifer and tormented by a gadfly sent by Hera

explanation.surface: A gadabout is the motion of an insect's prey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gadabout' is split as 'gad about', the word 'about' turning GAD into DAG.
explanation.definitionFit: A slow section of a symphony or sonata, marked by its tempo.

clue.text: Undertow that's punishing?

parts.note: a pull underneath a ship, dragging a sailor along its bottom as a naval penalty

explanation.surface: A dangerous current beneath the waves.
explanation.walkthrough: Undertow suggests a sea current; read as 'tow under', it is the old naval punishment of hauling a man under the hull.
explanation.definitionFit: The naval punishment of dragging an offender beneath a ship from side to side.

clue.text: A drug he takes the boy (such as Romeo)

definitions.text: A drug he takes the boy (such as Romeo)

parts.words: A drug he takes the boy (such as Romeo)
parts.note: in Shakespeare a seller of medicines provides the poison that a young lover like Romeo takes

explanation.surface: A man brings a narcotic to a young lover.
explanation.walkthrough: In Romeo and Juliet a poor seller of medicines in Mantua sells Romeo the poison he drinks; the clue also starts A, POT (drug) and HE.
explanation.definitionFit: An old word for a pharmacist, one who prepared and sold medicines.

clue.text: Work girls come out in lumps

indicators.note: the girls open out so that the work sits inside them

parts.note: dolls is slang for girls
op, short for opus, is a work

explanation.surface: Working girls break out in swellings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'come out in' looks like breaking out in a rash; here it opens DOLLS to take OP.
explanation.definitionFit: Shapeless masses or blobs, as of jam or mashed potato.

clue.text: Far from being left in defeat

parts.note: the opposite of left is right, abbreviated R
far from being in is to be out

explanation.surface: Someone is anything but stranded, in a heavy loss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Far from' applies to both 'being left' (right, R) and 'in' (OUT).
explanation.definitionFit: A crushing loss that sends the beaten side running in disorder.

clue.text: It's just fun and games with swings and roundabouts

parts.note: swings and roundabouts are rides at a fair
fun and games is play

explanation.surface: A day of rides and frolics described as entirely innocent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'swings and roundabouts' is the British saying about gains balancing losses; here they are fairground rides.
explanation.definitionFit: Equitable, sporting conduct is what justice in a contest consists of.

clue.text: Russian cleaners on British merchantmen

parts.note: red stands for Soviet Russian
dusters are cleaning cloths

explanation.surface: Russian cleaning staff aboard British trading vessels.
explanation.walkthrough: The red ensign, the flag of the British merchant navy, is nicknamed the red duster; the plural stands for the ships flying it.
explanation.definitionFit: The red ensign is flown by the British merchant fleet, so its sailor's nickname stands for trading ships.

clue.text: Are not perhaps the embellishments overdone?

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the words might be arranged some other way, so their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A critic asks whether the decoration on something has been laid on too thick.
explanation.definitionFit: Something florid or showy has decoration piled on to excess.

clue.text: St. Lazare chicken?

parts.note: the Paris station is the Gare St-Lazare, so a chicken there would be a station bird, which names an extinct seabird

explanation.surface: A bird found at a Paris railway terminus.
explanation.walkthrough: GARE is French for a railway station (the Gare St-Lazare in Paris), and FOWL is a chicken; together they name the great auk, a flightless seabird hunted to extinction.
explanation.definitionFit: This old name belongs to the great auk, a large flightless bird of the North Atlantic, extinct since the 1840s.

clue.text: Belted the young shaver ?

explanation.surface: A boy was given a thrashing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Young shaver' is slang for a boy, but here it is read as someone about to shave, covered in soap foam.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for thrashed or beaten; also covered in shaving foam, as a novice at the razor would be.

clue.text: Worn long ago to the scene of Sherman's march

parts.note: General Sherman's Civil War march to the sea crossed Georgia, abbreviated GA

explanation.surface: Something dressed in long ago, heading for the Civil War battleground.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman citizen's draped outer garment was clothing of the ancient world.

clue.text: Little Tom's men in the torture-chamber

parts.note: Tom Thumb is the tiny hero of the nursery tale
a crew is a body of men

explanation.surface: A tiny boy's companions in a dungeon.
explanation.definitionFit: An instrument of torture that crushes the digits, found in a dungeon.

clue.text: It might seem cop led the philosopher astray

indicators.note: going astray means wandering off course, so these letters stray into a new order

explanation.surface: A policeman seems to have misled a thinker.
explanation.definitionFit: He was a Greek thinker of Sicily who held that all matter is made of four elements.

clue.text: Going through all the cases

parts.note: reciting every grammatical case of a noun, as in Latin lessons, rather than examining legal cases

explanation.surface: Someone working through every file or lawsuit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cases' suggests lawsuits or files, but they are grammatical cases: nominative, accusative and the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: The full set of inflected forms of a noun or adjective in grammar.

clue.text: Foreign article in a foreign tin is filthy

parts.note: un is French for a

indicators.note: the French article is placed inside the other pieces

parts.note: a can is a tin
le is the French definite article

explanation.surface: Something imported in a can from abroad turns out to be dirty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts LE inside UNCAN, between the C and the A.
explanation.definitionFit: Dirty or impure, as in unwashed or ritually defiled.

clue.text: Many increase egg production with a sword

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral 100, a large number
hens that increase egg production lay more

explanation.surface: Lots of farmers boost egg yields using a blade.
explanation.definitionFit: The great two-handed broadsword of the Scottish Highlanders.

clue.text: Churchman gets a pass, yet goes wrong

parts.note: a col is a mountain pass

indicators.note: going wrong means going awry, so the letters of yet are jumbled

explanation.surface: A cleric is let through, but then things go badly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'goes wrong' turns YET into YTE.
explanation.definitionFit: An altar server or assistant in church services, a minor ecclesiastical office.

clue.text: A man of action

parts.note: action read as a lawsuit, so the man is a party to one in court rather than a doer

explanation.surface: Describes an energetic, decisive man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'action' suggests vigour; in law an action is a lawsuit.
explanation.definitionFit: A party to a lawsuit, someone suing or being sued.

clue.text: Rock 'n roll player? Certainly the latter

definitions.text: Rock 'n roll player? Certainly the latter

parts.words: Rock 'n roll player? Certainly the latter
parts.note: a musician of rock and roll? Not rock, but certainly roll: a piano played from a perforated paper roll

explanation.surface: Asks whether someone is a pop musician.
explanation.walkthrough: Rock 'n roll suggests pop music; 'the latter' picks out the roll, the perforated paper roll that drives a mechanical piano.
explanation.definitionFit: A mechanical player piano operated by a perforated paper roll.

clue.text: Was Howe drunk with victory here ?

definitions.text: Was Howe drunk with victory here ?

parts.words: Was Howe drunk with victory here ?
parts.note: General Howe beat Washington at a 1777 battle on a Pennsylvania creek whose name sounds like two drinks, spirits and the juice of the grape

explanation.surface: Asks whether a British general celebrated his win by getting tipsy.
explanation.walkthrough: The battle of 1777 on Brandywine Creek was won by the British commander Sir William Howe; the creek's name combines two drinks, hence 'drunk'.
explanation.definitionFit: The creek in Pennsylvania where the British won a major engagement of the American War of Independence.

clue.text: They're the end, if they don't come off of course

definitions.text: They're the end, if they don't come off of course

parts.words: They're the end, if they don't come off of course
parts.note: points or extremities are ends, and a punter's racing forecasts are a let-down when they fail on the racecourse

explanation.surface: Something is hopeless when it fails to work, naturally.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of course' reads as 'naturally' but means 'on the racecourse': a racing forecast that does not come off is a loss.
explanation.definitionFit: Ends or points of things, and also betting forecasts given for horse races.

clue.text: Military movement a bit crab-like ?

explanation.surface: An army manoeuvre with something of the crustacean about it.
explanation.walkthrough: A pincer movement is an attack closing on both flanks; a crab's claw is its pincer, a bit of a crab.
explanation.definitionFit: A two-pronged military attack that closes on the enemy, and also a claw that is part of a crab.

clue.text: The moping owl does to the moon (Gray)

definitions.text: The moping owl does to the moon

parts.words: The moping owl does to the moon
parts.note: a quotation from Thomas Gray's Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard, with its final word left as a blank to fill

explanation.surface: A line of verse with its last word missing, credited to the poet Gray.
explanation.walkthrough: The line in Gray's Elegy reads 'The moping owl does to the moon complain', so the missing word is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To grumble or lament, which the owl in the poem does to the moon.

clue.text: Did he have a whale of a time with Jezebel?

definitions.text: Did he have a whale of a time with Jezebel?

parts.words: Did he have a whale of a time with Jezebel?
parts.note: the name is shared by Melville's whale-hunting sea captain and the Old Testament king of Israel married to Jezebel

explanation.surface: Asks whether a man enjoyed himself with a wicked woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'whale of a time' means great fun, but it points to the captain chasing Moby Dick; the same name belongs to Jezebel's husband, a king in the Book of Kings.
explanation.definitionFit: The biblical king married to Jezebel, and Melville's captain obsessed with a white whale.

clue.text: Government man backs rock in Hilo

indicators.note: backs means going backwards, so everything built from the rock and the town is read in reverse
the rock is set inside the name of the Hawaiian town

parts.note: Hilo is a town in Hawaii, taken as written
a crag is a rock

explanation.surface: A politician supports a rock formation in a Hawaiian town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts CRAG inside HILO to give HCRAGILO, and 'backs' turns that whole string round.
explanation.definitionFit: A member of a small ruling clique, one of the few who govern.

clue.text: Bath discovery proclamation

parts.note: Archimedes, finding in his tub how to measure volume, cried out in triumph at the discovery

explanation.surface: An announcement of something found in the English spa city.
explanation.walkthrough: Bath suggests the English spa city, but it is the tub in which Archimedes saw displaced water and shouted Greek for 'I have found it'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek cry 'I have found it', attributed to Archimedes, announcing a discovery.

clue.text: Infernal downpour causes mental disturbance

parts.note: B is the printed initial of a coy oath such as blasted or bloody, which means infernal
a downpour is a heavy rainstorm

explanation.surface: Terrible weather is upsetting someone's state of mind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Infernal' gives B, the initial old papers printed for an oath (b----y), here spelling a sudden fit of madness.
explanation.definitionFit: In older use a sudden fit of madness or violent mental upset.
